items.stem: Grasshopper in grassland is a

options.label: A
options.text: producer

options.label: B
options.text: herbivore

options.label: C
options.text: carnivore

options.label: D
options.text: none of the above

items.answer: The plant is the producer and the animals are consumers. The first consumer in the chain is called the primary consumer, the next one the secondary consumer and the one after that the tertiary consumer. A consumer that eats plants is called a herbivore (grasshopper), and a consumer that eats other animals is called a carnivore (frog and hawk). An omnivore is an animal that eats both plants and animals. Thus (b) is the correct option.
items.ocr: Printed question number was dropped by OCR; inferred as 4 from its position between Q3 and Q5. Option label (c) was mangled to a bare 'C carnivore' and has been restored.

items.stem: Vultures in an ecosystem are

options.label: A
options.text: predators

options.label: B
options.text: scavengers

options.label: C
options.text: consumers

options.label: D
options.text: top carnivores

items.answer: Vultures are scavenging birds that feed on dead animals. Vultures do not kill their own prey, they feed on dead animals. As scavengers, vultures play an important role in the ecosystem by decomposing the dead animal matter, cleaning the environment and reducing the spread of diseases. Thus (b) is the correct option.
items.ocr: Option label (c) was dropped by OCR (printed as a bare 'consumers'); restored as option C.

items.stem: What must be preserved in an ecosystem, if the system needs to be maintained?

options.label: A
options.text: Producers and carnivores

options.label: B
options.text: Producers and decomposers

options.label: C
options.text: Carnivores and decomposers

options.label: D
options.text: Herbivores and carnivores

items.answer: The most important characteristics of any ecosystem are energy flow and cycling of materials. Producers and decomposers are indispensable for any ecosystem. Producers trap solar energy and convert it into a usable form as carbohydrates, which are passed on to successive levels through food chains and food webs. The other important characteristic of the ecosystem is the cycling of materials, called the bio-geochemical cycles, in which decomposers are the most important because they release the mineral nutrients back to the environment. Thus (b) is the correct option.
items.ocr: The 'Ans' line prints no key letter; the worked solution names option (b).

items.stem: What are trophic levels? Why do different food chains in an ecosystem not have more than four to five trophic levels? Give reason.
items.answer: Trophic level: the various steps or links or organisms in a food chain at which the transfer of food energy takes place are termed trophic levels. There is only a 10% flow of energy from one trophic level to the next higher level. The loss of energy at each step is so large that very little usable energy remains after four or five trophic levels. Hence only 4 to 5 trophic levels are present in each food chain.

items.stem:
Write any two differences between biodegradable and non-biodegradable substances by giving one example of each from our daily life.
Or
Differentiate between biodegradable and non-biodegradable pollutants. Classify the following under the above two categories: DDT, Paper, Cotton cloth, Plastic.
items.answer:
Biodegradable substances are broken down into simple and harmless substances by the action of micro-organisms; they are obtained from living things and do not cause environmental pollution. Examples: paper, cotton, clothes, vegetable peels. Non-biodegradable substances are not acted upon by micro-organisms and hence cannot be broken down into simpler forms; they persist and cause environmental pollution. Examples: plastic, glass, DDT. Classification: Biodegradable - Paper, Cotton cloth. Non-biodegradable - DDT, Plastic.
Biodegradable SubstancesNon-Biodegradable Substances

2.These are obtained from living things.These are obtained from non-living things.
3.They do not cause environmental pollution. Example: Paper, Cotton, Clothes, Vegetable peels etc.They cause environmental pollution. Example: Plastic, Glass, DDT etc.

items.stem: Government of India is imposing a ban on the use of polythene bags. List four advantages of using cloth or jute bags over polythene bags.
items.answer: Advantages of jute and cloth bags are: (i) They are re-usable. (ii) They are biodegradable. (iii) They are stronger than polythene bags and can carry more load. (iv) They can be repaired at home if torn.
items.ocr: The stem printed as 'Government of India is imposing ban on the use of polythene bags for stopping. List for advantages ...' - the dangling 'for stopping' was dropped and 'List for advantages' read as 'List four advantages', which the four-point answer confirms.

items.stem: Pesticides like DDT which are sprayed to kill pests on crops are found to be present in the soil, ground water, water bodies etc. Explain how do they reach these places.
items.answer:
Soil: Pesticides like DDT are used to protect crop plants from insects and pests. When sprayed on the plants they finally settle on the soil particles and cause soil pollution.
Ground water: Through irrigation the pesticides present in the soil pass into the lower layers of the soil, reach the ground water and pollute it.
Water bodies: When waste water or other agricultural waste is thrown, or runs off with rain water, into water bodies like rivers, canals and ponds, the pesticides reach these water bodies and pollute them.

items.stem:
In the following food chain, 5 J of energy is available to man. How much energy was available at producer level?
Plant → Sheep → Man
items.answer: Plant → Sheep → Man. The energy available to man in the above food chain is 5 J. According to the 10% law, the energy available to the sheep is 50 J. Again according to the 10% law, the energy available to the plants, i.e. at the producer level, is 500 J.
items.ocr: LaTeX artefacts rewritten: '$5 \textup{J}$' and '$5{}]$' to 5 J, '$50 \mathrm{J}$' to 50 J, '$10\%$' to 10%. MinerU dropped the food-chain arrows (printed 'Plant $$ Sheep $$ Man'); restored as Plant → Sheep → Man.
